tips.title: Job, batch, flow — one, some, many
tips.body: **Job** makes **one** item to order. **Batch** makes **a group** of identical items then changes over. **Flow** makes **many**, continuously. Match the process to how similar the products are and how many are wanted.

tips.title: Read a stock graph at the sawtooth
tips.body: Stock **falls** as it is used and **jumps** when a delivery arrives. The **lowest** points are the **buffer stock**, the **highest** are the **maximum**, and the level where the line turns out to have triggered an order is the **reorder level**.

tips.title: Control inspects, assurance prevents
tips.body: **Quality control** checks the product **at the end** and rejects faults. **Quality assurance** builds quality in **at every stage**, so faults are prevented rather than caught. One finds; the other stops.

tips.title: JIT trades stock for risk
tips.body: Just in time cuts **storage costs** and frees up **cash**, but leaves **no buffer**. One late supplier stops production. Always name both halves — the saving and the exposure.

tips.title: Apply it to the business in the question
tips.body: Edexcel marks **application**. Naming the process is Level 1; saying why **this** business, with **these** products and **this** order size, should use it is what moves an answer up the levels.

steps.title: What business operations are for
steps.body:
**The purpose of business operations is to produce goods or to provide services.** Everything in this topic is about doing that well: making the right things, to the right quality, at a cost that allows a competitive price.

**Operations decisions matter because they decide the cost of each unit.** A business that produces efficiently can either charge less than its rivals or keep a wider margin at the same price. Either way the advantage comes from operations, not from marketing.

**They also decide what the customer actually receives** — whether the product works, arrives on time, and matches what was promised. Operations is where a marketing promise is either kept or broken.

**The running example.** *Pike & Pine* is a workshop making wooden furniture. It sells bespoke dining tables, runs of matching chairs, and is considering a simple flat-pack shelf for a larger retailer. That gives it a reason to use every production process in the specification, and its decisions will be used throughout.

points: it sets the cost per unit

check.prompt: What is the purpose of business operations?

To advertise the business to customers
To raise finance for expansion
To recruit and train employees
check.solution: Operations exists **to produce goods or provide services**. Advertising is marketing, raising finance is finance, and recruitment is human resources.

steps.title: Job, batch and flow production
steps.body:
**The specification names three production processes.**

**Job production** makes **one item at a time**, to order, from start to finish. A bespoke dining table for one customer. The work is skilled, the product can be exactly what the customer asked for, and the **cost per unit is high** because nothing is repeated.

**Batch production** makes **a group of identical items together**, then changes the equipment over for the next group. Forty chairs in one oak finish, then forty in walnut. It is more efficient than job production because the set-up is shared across the batch, and still flexible enough to offer variety. The **changeover time between batches** is its main cost.

**Flow production** moves items **continuously along a production line**. Flat-pack shelving, made by the thousand. The **cost per unit is lowest**, because the line never stops and the set-up is spread across enormous volume. It needs **high demand** and **heavy investment**, and it is inflexible — changing the product means stopping the line.

**The trade is always the same: flexibility against cost per unit.** Job production is the most flexible and the most expensive per item; flow is the least flexible and the cheapest.

steps.title: Choosing a process, and keeping costs down
steps.body:
**The specification asks for the impact of the different processes: keeping productivity up and costs down and allowing for competitive prices.**

**Productivity** is output per worker in a given time. Higher productivity means each unit carries **less labour cost**, so the unit cost falls and the business can either cut its price or keep more margin.

**How the process affects it.** Flow production has the highest productivity because the work is repeated and nothing is set up twice. Job production has the lowest, because every item starts again. Batch sits between them, and the **changeover** is where its productivity is lost.

**Pike & Pine's decision.** A bespoke table must be **job** production — there is one of it, and the customer chose the dimensions. Chairs sold in matching sets suit **batch**: forty at a time in one finish shares the set-up. The flat-pack shelf for a retailer would need **flow**, because the volume is high and every unit is identical.

**Getting it wrong is expensive both ways.** Using job production for the shelves would make them far too costly to sell at a retailer's price. Using flow production for bespoke tables is impossible — there is nothing to repeat.

**So the question to ask is: how similar are the products, and how many are wanted?** That answers the process almost every time.

check.prompt: Why does flow production give the lowest cost per unit?
options: The set-up cost is spread across a very large output
Each item is made individually by a skilled worker
The equipment is changed over between every item
It uses fewer materials than the other processes
check.solution: Flow repeats the same work continuously, so the **set-up is spread across enormous volume** and little time is lost. Making each item individually is **job** production, which has the **highest** unit cost.

steps.title: Technology in production
steps.body:
**The specification frames this exactly: the impact of technology on production is about balancing cost, productivity, quality and flexibility.** All four, not just cost.

**Productivity.** A machine works faster and does not tire, so output per worker rises. If Pike & Pine buys a computer-controlled cutter, 5 workers producing 60 chairs a week move to 90 — productivity rises from **12** to **18** chairs per worker, a rise of **50%**.

**Quality.** A machine repeats the same cut to the same tolerance every time, so there is **less variation** and fewer faults. Consistency is often the bigger gain, because it is what customers notice.

**Cost.** This cuts both ways. The **unit cost falls** once the machine is running, but the machine must be **bought, maintained and repaired**, and staff must be **retrained**. A business with low output may never recover the purchase price.

**Flexibility.** This is the one students forget, and it can go **either way**. Some technology makes a business *more* flexible — a computer-controlled cutter can switch design in software. Other technology makes it *less* flexible: a production line built for one product is expensive to change.

**So "technology is good because it is faster" is a Level 1 answer.** The marks are in naming which of the four is affected, in which direction, **for this business**.

rows: only if there is demand for the extra output
a fault in the setting repeats every time too
purchase, maintenance and retraining come first
a line built for one product is hard to change
props.title: All four, and flexibility is the one most often left out

check.solution: Productivity is output per worker: $90 \div 5 = $ **18** chairs per worker per week.

steps.title: Reading a bar gate stock graph
steps.body: **A bar gate stock graph shows stock falling as it is used and jumping when a delivery arrives** — a sawtooth. Pike & Pine uses 100 metres of oak a week, holds a maximum of 400 metres, and its supplier takes 1 week to deliver.

visuals.problem: Read the stock graph and explain each level.

steps.text: The **maximum stock level** is the highest point: **400 metres**
steps.note: the most the business is willing or able to hold at once

steps.text: Stock falls by the **usage rate** of 100 metres a week: 400 → 300 → 200 → 100
steps.note: the downward slope of the sawtooth is the usage rate

steps.text: The **reorder level** is **200 metres**, reached in week 2 — the order is placed here
steps.note: not when stock runs out; the order must be placed with time to arrive

steps.text: **Lead time** is 1 week, during which another 100 metres are used
steps.note: lead time is the gap between placing the order and receiving it

steps.text: So stock bottoms out at **100 metres** — the **buffer stock**, held back for emergencies
steps.note: reorder level (200) minus usage during lead time (100) = buffer (100)

steps.text: The delivery of **300 metres** arrives and takes stock back to 400
steps.note: 400 − 100 = 300 — the order size refills to the maximum, no further

rows: maximum stock level, just after delivery
reorder level reached — the order is placed
buffer stock; the delivery arrives and stock returns to 400
props.title: Reorder level minus usage during lead time gives the buffer: 200 − 100 = 100

visuals.alt: A table walking a bar gate stock graph week by week from maximum stock down to buffer stock

check.prompt: A business reorders at 200 units, uses 100 units a week, and its supplier takes 1 week. What is its buffer stock?
check.solution: During the 1 week lead time it uses 100 units, so stock falls from 200 to **100**. The buffer stock is the level it bottoms out at.

markScheme.description: uses usage × lead time

steps.title: Just in time stock control
steps.body:
**Just in time (JIT)** means holding **as little stock as possible** and arranging for materials to arrive **exactly when they are needed**.

**What it saves.** Storage space and its cost. Cash that would otherwise sit on a shelf as unused timber. Waste from stock that is damaged, stolen or goes out of date. For a business with limited space and limited cash, those are large gains.

**What it costs.** There is **no buffer**. If one delivery is late, production **stops**, because there is nothing held back. Deliveries are also **more frequent and smaller**, so delivery costs rise and bulk discounts are lost.

**What it depends on.** JIT only works with **reliable suppliers** and good relationships. It shifts the risk from the business's warehouse onto its supply chain, which is fine until the supply chain is disrupted.

**For Pike & Pine**, JIT would free up cash and workshop space. But a single late timber delivery would idle 5 workers who still have to be paid, and a customer waiting on a bespoke table would be told it is late. Whether that trade is worth taking depends on **how reliable the supplier is**, which is why this topic leads straight into procurement.

**In the exam, never give JIT as simply "better".** Name the saving **and** the exposure, and say which matters more for the business in front of you.

props.title: JIT moves the risk out of the warehouse and into the supply chain

visuals.alt: A table comparing holding buffer stock with just in time across five factors

check.prompt: What is the main risk of just in time stock control?
options: A late delivery stops production, as there is no buffer
Stock becomes damaged while held in storage
Too much cash is tied up in unused materials
Bulk discounts make the materials more expensive
check.solution: JIT holds **no buffer**, so one late delivery halts production. Damaged stock and cash tied up are problems of **holding** stock — exactly what JIT avoids.

markScheme.description: a late delivery stops production

steps.title: Working with suppliers
steps.body:
**Procurement is the business of buying what the business needs to operate.** The specification lists what matters in a supplier relationship: **quality, delivery (cost, speed, reliability), availability, cost, trust**.

**Quality** — poor materials become poor products, and the customer blames the business, not the supplier.

**Delivery** has three parts worth separating. **Cost**: what delivery adds to the price. **Speed**: how quickly it arrives. **Reliability**: whether it arrives **when promised**. Reliability matters more than speed for a business running JIT, because a plan can work around a slow supplier but not an unpredictable one.

**Availability** — can the supplier meet a larger order if the business grows, or at a busy time of year?

**Cost** — the price paid feeds straight into the cost per unit and therefore into the margin.

**Trust** — the underpinning of the rest. A trusted supplier warns you when there is a problem, gives credit terms, and prioritises you when stock is short.

**The cheapest supplier is not always the best choice**, and saying so is worth marks. A supplier £2 a metre cheaper but occasionally a week late could cost Pike & Pine far more in idle workers and missed delivery dates than the saving is worth.

boxes.title: Availability and cost
points: can they supply more if you grow?

visuals.alt: A four-box card on what matters when choosing a supplier: quality, delivery, availability, cost and trust

check.prompt: Why might a business reject the cheapest supplier?
options: Unreliable delivery could cost more than the saving
Cheaper suppliers are not allowed under procurement rules
A low price always means the materials are unusable
Cheaper suppliers cannot deliver in large quantities
check.solution: Price is only one of the factors. A cheaper supplier who is **late or inconsistent** can cost far more in stopped production, missed deadlines and lost customers than the lower price saves.

markScheme.description: unreliable delivery can cost more than the saving

steps.title: Logistics and its effects
steps.body:
**The specification asks for the impact of logistics and supply decisions on three things: costs, reputation and customer satisfaction.** Learn them as a trio — a question will usually want more than one.

**Costs.** Transport, storage, handling and insurance all feed into the cost per unit. Choosing a distant supplier to save on price may give the saving back in delivery charges. Frequent small deliveries under JIT cost more per unit delivered than a few large ones.

**Reputation.** This is the one that outlasts the incident. A business that misses delivery dates becomes known for it, and a reputation for lateness is far harder to repair than the original delay. Reviews and word of mouth make a single bad experience visible to people who were never affected by it.

**Customer satisfaction.** Late, damaged or incomplete deliveries mean unhappy customers, complaints, refunds, and customers who do not return. A product can be excellent and the customer still dissatisfied because it arrived a fortnight late.

**Notice the chain**, because chains of reasoning are what Edexcel's levels reward: a supply decision → a delivery problem → an unhappy customer → a poor review → fewer future customers → lower revenue. Each arrow is a link, and an answer that follows the chain to **revenue or profit** scores higher than one that stops at "customers would be annoyed".

rows: fewer delays if supply is reliable
orders fulfilled even when supply fails
props.title: Follow the chain to revenue or profit — that is what the levels reward

visuals.alt: A table of four supply decisions with their effects on costs and on customers

check.prompt: Why is damage to reputation often worse than the original late delivery?
options: A reputation for lateness is hard to repair and reaches new customers
Reputation damage is always compensated by refunds
Late deliveries do not affect the customers involved
Reputation only matters to businesses selling online
check.solution: The late delivery affects **one** customer. A reputation for lateness — through reviews and word of mouth — reaches **people who were never affected**, and it persists long after the original problem is fixed.

markScheme.description: it is hard to repair and reaches new customers

steps.title: Quality control and quality assurance
steps.body:
**Quality means the product or service meets the standard the customer expects.** The specification names two ways of managing it, and the difference is examined directly.

**Quality control (QC)** — the finished product is **inspected at the end**, and faulty items are rejected or reworked. Quality is checked **by inspectors**, and it is checked **after the work is done**.

**Quality assurance (QA)** — quality is built in **at every stage**, with **each worker responsible** for checking their own work before passing it on. Faults are **prevented** rather than caught.

**Why QA is usually preferred.** Under QC, a fault made at the first stage has work added to it all the way down the line before anyone notices — so all of that work is wasted too. Under QA it is caught immediately, when only one stage of work is lost. QA also tends to raise the standard generally, because responsibility sits with the person doing the work rather than with someone at the end.

**QC is not worthless.** It needs less training, works where individual skill matters less, and gives a final guarantee that nothing faulty leaves the building. Many businesses use both.

**A memory hook:** **control catches, assurance prevents.**

rows: every worker, for their own work
all work added after the fault
only the stage where it occurred
training and a culture of responsibility
props.title: Control catches; assurance prevents

visuals.alt: A table comparing quality control and quality assurance across five properties

check.prompt: What is the main difference between quality assurance and quality control?
options: Assurance builds quality in at every stage; control inspects at the end
Assurance applies to services and control applies to goods
Assurance is carried out by customers rather than employees
Assurance costs nothing whereas control is expensive
check.solution: **Assurance** builds quality in throughout, with each worker checking their own work, so faults are **prevented**. **Control** inspects the finished item and **catches** faults at the end.

markScheme.description: assurance builds in at every stage, control inspects at the end

steps.title: Why quality pays
steps.body:
**The specification says quality allows a business to control costs and gain a competitive advantage.** Both halves are worth explaining.

**Controlling costs.** Poor quality is expensive in ways that are easy to miss. Faulty items are **scrapped or reworked**, so the materials and labour are paid for twice. Returns cost postage, handling and refunds. Complaints take staff time. Warranty repairs come out of profit. A business that gets it right first time avoids all of it.

**Competitive advantage.** Reliable quality lets a business charge a **higher price**, because customers will pay more for something that works and lasts. It builds **repeat custom** and **recommendations**, which are far cheaper than advertising. And it **differentiates** the business from cheaper rivals, which matters most when it cannot compete on price.

**For Pike & Pine this is the whole strategy.** A workshop cannot beat a factory on price, so its case for costing more has to be that the furniture is better made and lasts longer. If quality slips, it is left charging a high price for an ordinary product — the worst position to be in.

**The chain to finish on:** better quality → fewer returns and higher prices → higher margin and repeat custom → higher profit. That is the reasoning the top level is looking for.

boxes.title: Position
points: essential if you cannot win on price

visuals.alt: A four-box card on how quality controls costs and creates competitive advantage

check.prompt: How does high quality help a business control its costs?
options: Fewer faults mean less scrap, rework and fewer returns
High quality materials are always cheaper to buy
Quality removes the need to employ any inspectors
Better quality products need less advertising by law
check.solution: Faults are paid for **twice** — once to make the item and again to scrap or rework it — plus returns, refunds and complaint handling. Getting it right first time avoids all of those costs.

markScheme.description: less scrap, rework and fewer returns

steps.title: The sales process
steps.body:
**The specification lists five parts of the sales process**, and asks why good customer service matters.

**Product knowledge** — staff who understand what they are selling can answer questions, match the customer to the right product, and be believed. A customer who is given a wrong answer usually does not buy.

**Speed and efficiency of service** — customers who wait too long leave. Efficiency also lowers cost, because staff time is the expense.

**Customer engagement** — treating the customer as a person: listening, taking an interest, remembering them. It is what makes a small business worth choosing over a cheaper website.

**Responses to customer feedback** — acting on what customers say, whether a complaint or a suggestion. A complaint handled well often leaves the customer **more** loyal than if nothing had gone wrong; ignored, it becomes a public review.

**Post-sales service** — support after the purchase: delivery, installation, warranties, repairs, spare parts. For an expensive item this is often what decided the purchase in the first place.

**Why good customer service matters.** It creates **repeat custom**, and keeping a customer is much cheaper than finding a new one. It generates **recommendations**. It allows a **higher price**, because service is part of what is being bought. And for a business that cannot compete on price — Pike & Pine against a furniture warehouse — it may be the main reason anyone chooses it at all.

why a person beats a cheaper website

visuals.alt: A table of the five parts of the sales process, what each means and why it matters

check.prompt: Which part of the sales process covers delivery, warranties and repairs after the customer has bought?
check.solution: **Post-sales service** — the support given after the purchase, which for an expensive item is often what persuaded the customer to buy in the first place.

markScheme.description: post-sales service

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
*Pike & Pine* makes wooden furniture. It uses 100 metres of oak a week, holds a maximum of 400 metres, and reorders at 200 metres. Its supplier takes 1 week to deliver.

**Part A.**

1. State the purpose of business operations.
2. Name the three production processes.
3. Name the two ways of managing quality.

**Part B.**

4. Which process should Pike & Pine use for a bespoke dining table, and why?
5. Using the figures above, state the buffer stock and the size of each delivery.
6. 5 workers produce 90 chairs a week. Calculate productivity per worker.

**Part C.**

7. Explain two factors other than price that Pike & Pine should consider when choosing a supplier.
8. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of just in time for Pike & Pine.
9. Evaluate whether Pike & Pine should invest in a computer-controlled cutter.

For question 9, use **all four** of cost, productivity, quality and flexibility, then judge.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Apply everything to the business in the question.** Edexcel marks **application**, and it is the difference between the levels. *Batch production is efficient* is Level 1. *Batch suits Pike & Pine because it sells chairs in matching sets of four to six, so a run of forty in one finish shares the set-up across enough units to cut the cost, while still letting it offer walnut next month* is Level 3.

**Follow the chain to profit.** A supply problem → a late delivery → an unhappy customer → a poor review → fewer customers → **lower revenue**. Stopping at "customers would be annoyed" leaves marks behind; the levels explicitly reward **chains of reasoning that connect points**.

**Read a stock graph from its shape.** The **highest** points are the maximum, the **lowest** are the buffer, the **downward slope** is the usage rate, and the **vertical jump** is a delivery. Reorder level minus usage during lead time gives the buffer — 200 − 100 = 100 here.

**Never present JIT as simply better.** Name the saving — storage cost, cash freed, less waste — **and** the exposure: no buffer, so one late delivery stops production. Then say which matters more **for this business**, which usually turns on how reliable its suppliers are.

**Be exact on quality.** **Control catches** at the end; **assurance prevents** at every stage. The strongest point is about **wasted work**: under QC a fault made early has value added to it all the way down the line before anyone notices, so everything after the fault is wasted too.

**Use all four technology factors.** Cost, productivity, quality **and flexibility**. Flexibility is the one students drop, and it is the one that can go **either way** — software-driven machines increase it, a dedicated line reduces it.

**Say the cheapest supplier may not be the best.** Weigh **reliability** against **price**, with a figure if the question gives you one. A saving of £2 a metre is worthless if a week's delay idles 5 workers who are still paid.

**Reach a judgement that names what it depends on.** *Pike & Pine should buy the cutter provided it can sell the extra 30 chairs a week* is a conclusion. *There are advantages and disadvantages* is not.

rows: named to this business and its products
follows through to revenue or profit
the saving and the exposure, then a judgement
a judgement naming what it depends on
props.title: The first two rows are where most of the levels marks are won and lost

visuals.alt: A table of common errors in operational decisions answers and what earns the marks instead

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Operations exists **to produce goods or provide services**.
- **Job** makes one to order — most flexible, **highest** cost per unit.
- **Batch** makes a group, then changes over — the **changeover** is its cost.
- **Flow** runs continuously — **lowest** unit cost, least flexible, needs high demand.
- **Productivity** is output per worker; higher productivity lowers unit cost.
- Technology balances **cost, productivity, quality and flexibility** — all four.
- Flexibility can **rise or fall** with technology.
- On a stock graph: highest = **maximum**, lowest = **buffer**, slope = **usage**, jump = **delivery**.
- **Reorder level − usage during lead time = buffer stock** (200 − 100 = 100).
- **JIT** cuts storage cost and frees cash, but leaves **no buffer**.
- Supplier factors: **quality, delivery (cost, speed, reliability), availability, cost, trust**.
- The **cheapest supplier is not always the best**.
- Logistics affects **costs, reputation and customer satisfaction**.
- **Quality control catches** at the end; **quality assurance prevents** at every stage.
- The sales process: **product knowledge, speed and efficiency, customer engagement, responses to feedback, post-sales service**.

reorder level − usage in lead time
no buffer, so a late delivery stops production

A delayed order is always cancelled by the customer

questions.solution: The delay itself costs one order. The **reputation** spreads through reviews and word of mouth to people who never placed an order at all, and it persists long after the supply problem is fixed — so the lost revenue continues.

markScheme.description: reviews reach customers never affected

questions.prompt: A workshop cannot match a factory's prices. Why does quality become central to its strategy?
options: It must justify a higher price by being better made
Quality is cheaper to achieve than low prices are
Small businesses are legally held to higher standards
High quality removes the need to advertise at all
questions.solution: If it cannot win on **price**, it must **differentiate**. Quality gives customers a reason to pay more, brings repeat custom and recommendations, and is what the higher price is for. Should quality slip, it is left charging more for an ordinary product — the worst position available.

markScheme.description: it must justify a higher price

questions.prompt: Why might a business use batch rather than flow production even when demand is high?
options: It needs to offer variety, which flow production cannot
Batch production always costs less per unit than flow
Flow production cannot be used for physical goods
Batch production requires no equipment set-up at all
questions.solution: Flow gives the lowest unit cost but is **inflexible** — the line makes one thing. If customers want several finishes or sizes, **batch** allows variety by changing over between runs. The set-up time is the price paid for that choice.

markScheme.description: batch allows variety that flow cannot

questions.prompt: Pike & Pine is a workshop making wooden furniture. It uses 100 metres of oak a week, holds a maximum of 400 metres and reorders at 200 metres; its supplier takes one week to deliver. It is considering moving to just in time stock control to free up cash and workshop space. Analyse whether Pike & Pine should adopt just in time.
questions.solution:
**Just in time (JIT)** means holding as little stock as possible, with materials arriving exactly when they are needed. For Pike & Pine that would mean abandoning its **100 metre buffer stock** and its 400 metre maximum, and taking oak in small deliveries as each job requires it.

**The benefits are real and specific to this business.** At present it holds up to **400 metres** of oak, which is cash sitting in the workshop doing nothing until it is cut. Releasing that cash would let the business buy equipment or simply survive a slow month. A workshop is also usually short of **space**, and timber storage takes a great deal of it — space that could hold another workbench and therefore more output. There is also less risk of stock being **damaged, warped or stolen** while it waits, which matters for timber in particular.

**The risks are equally specific.** Pike & Pine currently holds a **buffer of 100 metres**, which is a full week of production at its usage rate of 100 metres a week. That buffer exists precisely so that a late delivery does not stop work. Under JIT it would be gone, and since the supplier's **lead time is a week**, a single missed delivery would leave the workshop with nothing to cut and no way to fix it quickly.

The chain that follows is what makes this serious. A late delivery → **production stops** → the workers are **idle but still paid**, so costs continue while output is zero → a customer waiting on a bespoke table is told it will be late → that customer leaves a poor review → future customers who were never affected see it → **fewer orders and lower revenue**. For a small workshop trading on its reputation for care and reliability, that last step is the real damage, and it lasts far longer than the delay.

JIT would also mean **more frequent, smaller deliveries**, which cost more per metre delivered and forfeit any bulk discount — so some of the cash saving is given back.

**Judgement.** Whether Pike & Pine should adopt JIT depends almost entirely on **how reliable its supplier is**, because JIT does not remove the risk of supply failure — it moves it out of the workshop and into the supply chain. If the supplier has delivered on time consistently for years, the cash and space released are worth having. If deliveries are ever late, the buffer is doing exactly the job it exists for and should be kept.

On balance I would advise a **partial move**: reduce the maximum stock level to free up most of the cash and space, but retain a **smaller buffer** — perhaps two or three days of timber rather than a full week. That captures most of the benefit while leaving enough margin to absorb one late delivery, which is the failure this business cannot afford.

questions.prompt: Pike & Pine currently has 5 workers producing 60 chairs a week. A computer-controlled cutter costing £40,000 would raise output to 90 chairs a week with the same 5 workers, and would cut each chair to a more consistent finish. The workshop sells chairs at a higher price than factory-made ones because of their quality. Evaluate whether Pike & Pine should buy the cutter.
questions.solution:
**The case for buying the cutter** begins with **productivity**. At present 5 workers make 60 chairs a week, which is **12 chairs per worker**. With the cutter the same 5 workers would make 90, which is **18 per worker** — a rise of **50%**. Because the wage bill is unchanged, the **labour cost per chair falls by a third**, and that feeds straight into either a wider margin or the ability to hold prices while costs rise elsewhere.

The **quality** argument may matter more for this particular business. A computer-controlled cutter repeats the same cut to the same tolerance every time, so there is **less variation** between chairs. Pike & Pine sells at a **higher price than factory-made furniture on the strength of how well it is made**, so anything that makes the product more consistent supports the price it is charging. Fewer faults also means less **scrap and rework**, which is material and labour paid for twice.

There is a growth argument too: producing 30 more chairs a week without hiring anyone means the business can take larger orders, which may be what a retailer requires before placing one.

**The case against starts with the £40,000.** That is a large sum for a workshop, and it is spent before any benefit arrives. It may require a **loan**, with interest adding to fixed costs every month whether or not the extra chairs sell. There will also be **maintenance**, **repair** and **retraining** costs that the headline figure does not include.

The central risk is **demand**. The extra output is only worth anything if the chairs can be **sold**. Producing 30 more chairs a week that sit unsold converts cash into stock, takes up workshop space and achieves nothing — the productivity gain is only a gain if there are customers at the end of it. Before spending £40,000 the business needs evidence that the demand exists.

There is a subtler risk about the **brand**. Pike & Pine's premium rests on furniture being **hand-finished**. If customers come to see the work as machine-made, the reason they were paying more disappears, and the business finds itself competing with factories on their terms rather than its own. Against that, the cutter affects **cutting**, not finishing, so the hand-finished character can be preserved if the business is careful about what it automates and how it describes it.

**Flexibility** cuts in its favour here: a computer-controlled cutter switches design in **software**, so it should make bespoke work easier rather than harder — unlike a dedicated production line, which would lock the workshop into one product.

**Conclusion.** Pike & Pine should buy the cutter, but the decision depends on one thing above all: whether it can **sell the additional 30 chairs a week**. The productivity and quality gains are real and well matched to a business competing on quality rather than price, and the flexibility concern does not apply to this kind of machine.

So the sensible sequence is to secure the demand **first** — a retail order, or evidence of a waiting list — and buy the cutter against it. Spending £40,000 in the hope that demand follows would turn a sound investment into a serious cash-flow risk, and for a workshop of this size that is the mistake it would struggle to recover from.

examTechnique.body:
**Apply every point to the business named in the question** — Edexcel marks application, and a generic definition caps at Level 1. **Follow chains of reasoning through to revenue or profit** rather than stopping at "customers would be annoyed".

For stock graphs: highest is **maximum**, lowest is **buffer**, slope is **usage**, jump is a **delivery**. For technology, use all four of **cost, productivity, quality and flexibility**.
examinerErrors: Giving a textbook definition with no reference to the business in the question.
Stopping a chain at "customers would be unhappy" instead of reaching revenue or profit.
Presenting just in time as simply better, with no mention of the missing buffer.
Using quality control and quality assurance as if they meant the same thing.
Discussing technology only in terms of speed and cost, omitting flexibility.
Recommending the cheapest supplier without weighing reliability.
Confusing the reorder level with the buffer stock on a stock graph.
Ending with "there are advantages and disadvantages" and no judgement.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the business and its products in **every** paragraph, and uses the figures it was given. It builds **chains** — a supply decision leads to a delay, which leads to a review, which leads to lost revenue — rather than listing separate points. It presents **both sides** of JIT and technology, including **flexibility**, which most answers drop, and it knows that **control catches while assurance prevents**, explaining that a fault caught late wastes all the work added after it. It finishes with a **judgement that names what it depends on** — whether the supplier is reliable, or whether the extra output can actually be sold.
